wine.name: Grosset Polish Hill Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the Polish Hill River locality of the valley.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyard in the Polish Hill River locality, east of Sevenhill, at about 460 to 480 metres: silt and shallow shale over a thin crust of clay and gravel on blue slate, a hard rock site of small bunches and berries.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and only the free run juice is used, settled cold and fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel, then bottled young and unfined. No oak and no malolactic fermentation; the wine has been sealed under screwcap since the 2000 vintage.
wine.glass: Lime juice and lime zest, lemon blossom and green apple over a crushed slate note; bone dry and light in body, with high, tight acidity and a long, linear finish. Age brings toast and a honeyed edge to the lime.
wine.ageing: Tight and reserved when young, it opens slowly and keeps for a decade and more, longer and more austere than the house's Springvale.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, as an aperitif or with crab or grilled fish.

label.means: The locality east of Sevenhill where the vineyard lies; a local name, not a legal subregion.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The variety named on the label; at least 85 per cent of the wine must be made from it.

records.table: Grosset Polish Hill is a bone dry Clare Valley Riesling from shallow shale over blue slate in the Polish Hill River locality: lime, lemon blossom and a stony edge on tight, high acidity. It opens more slowly than the house's Springvale, so give it years.
records.story: Polish Hill River took its name from settlers: in 1856 the ship August brought more than a hundred Polish migrants to South Australia, and the largest group farmed by the Hill River east of Sevenhill, which came to be called Polish Hill River. In 1981 the founder, a young winemaker, set up his own winery at Auburn, at the southern end of the valley, in an old milk depot, by the house's own account. His first wines that year included two dry Rieslings, one from Watervale and one from Polish Hill fruit. In 1996 the house planted its own vineyard at Polish Hill, a hard rock site of shale over slate, certified organic and biodynamic by its own account. In 2000 the house led a group of fourteen Clare producers who bottled their Riesling under screwcap together, so that no one maker carried alone the risk of a closure many buyers then distrusted; screwcap became the valley's usual closure for Riesling. Polish Hill shows a sommelier what a site does to Riesling: beside the house's Watervale wine, Springvale, it is tighter, stonier and slower to open.

others.name: Springvale Riesling
others.note: The house's Watervale Riesling from limestone, more open, with lime blossom to the fore, and approachable earlier than Polish Hill.

others.name: Gaia
others.note: A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc from the house's Gaia vineyard high in the valley.

traps: Polish Hill River and Watervale are localities of the Clare Valley; the region has no legally defined subregions, so the geographical indication on the label is Clare Valley.
Clare dry Riesling is fully dry: expecting residual sugar is the standard error.
Polish Hill and Springvale are two sites of one house, not two tiers of quality.

wine.name: The Armagh Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the Armagh vineyard.
wine.sites: The Armagh vineyard, by the hamlet of Armagh near the town of Clare, on land the founder bought in 1964; its Shiraz was planted in the late 1960s, by the house's story from cuttings taken at Wendouree.
wine.making: Fermented on its skins, then matured in oak for well over a year, between about sixteen and twenty months by vintage in the house's records. The first vintage was aged in new American oak alone; French oak later joined it, and some vintages have seen French oak only.
wine.glass: Blackberry, mulberry and dark chocolate over mint and black pepper; full bodied and dense, with ripe, fine grained tannin, fresh acidity and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed for its first years, it wants a decade in a strong vintage and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Jim Barry Wines makes The Armagh from Shiraz the founder planted by the hamlet of Armagh in the late 1960s, first bottled under that name from the 1985 vintage. It is blackberry, dark chocolate and mint in a dense, full red, so decant it and use a large glass.
records.story: Jim Barry, who died in 2004 at the age of seventy nine, graduated from Roseworthy College in 1947 and went to the Clarevale co-operative, by most accounts the first qualified winemaker the Clare Valley had. In 1959 he and his wife bought their first property and founded Jim Barry Wines. In 1964 he bought land near the hamlet of Armagh, and planted Shiraz there at the end of the decade, from cuttings that by most accounts came from the old vines of Wendouree. In 1985, the year one of the founder's sons took charge of the company, another son made the first The Armagh from that Shiraz, aged in new American oak. In 1986 the family bought the Florita vineyard at Watervale from Lindemans, once the source of Leo Buring's Rieslings, and gave the house its Riesling to match the red. French oak later joined the American, and some vintages have seen French oak alone. In 2020 its 2016 vintage was offered through La Place de Bordeaux, the merchant system of Bordeaux, the first Australian Shiraz so sold. For a sommelier it is the answer to anyone who thinks Clare makes only Riesling.

others.note: Dry Riesling from the Watervale vineyard the family bought from Lindemans in 1986, once a source of Leo Buring's Rieslings.

Clare is not only a white region: The Armagh is dense, long lived Shiraz from the same valley as the house's Florita Riesling.
Watervale is a locality of the Clare Valley, not a separate geographical indication.

wine.name: Wendouree Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's own dry grown vineyard on clay at the southern end of the valley near Sevenhill, where the oldest Shiraz is told as planted in the 1890s and never grafted.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented in open fermenters with the cap plunged by hand, then pressed in an old basket press that runs on rails set in cement between the fermenters. The wine is matured in oak barrels, mostly seasoned, for about a year by one account, before it is bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Blackberry, mulberry and satsuma plum over mint, liquorice and an iron note; dense and full, with high, firm, drying tannin and fresh acidity in youth, turning to leather and dried mint with age.
wine.ageing: Fierce and closed in youth, it is seldom ready before ten to fifteen years and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The estate's name, given by the Birks family who planted it in the 1890s.

records.table: Wendouree Shiraz comes from dry grown vines near Sevenhill, some planted in the 1890s, made the old way in open vats and a basket press. It is dense and fiercely tannic when young, so keep it ten years and more and then decant it.
records.story: In the early 1890s a young man of the Birks family planted vines with his brother near Sevenhill and called the estate Wendouree. Accounts give 1892 or 1893 for the first vines, and the first Wendouree wines were released in 1895. In 1917, his health failing, the founder handed the winemaking to his son, who made its wine for more than half a century, selling much of it in cask to local hotels and trade and bottling little, through years when few drinkers wanted dense dry red. The Birks family kept Wendouree until 1974, when it was bought at a mortgagee sale and passed into the care of the buyer's daughter and son in law, who have changed very little: the vines are dry grown, the wine is made in open vats and a basket press, and nearly all of it is sold by letter to a mailing list. Because phylloxera has never been found in South Australia, the vines of the 1890s stand on their own roots, and the house of Jim Barry says its Armagh Shiraz was planted from cuttings taken here. To a sommelier Wendouree Shiraz is old Clare in the glass: dense, tannic and slow.

wine.name: Sevenhill St Ignatius
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about half, with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc for the rest.
wine.sites: Clare Valley fruit; the house's sheets read do not name the vineyards that give this blend.
wine.making: Each part is fermented on its skins for about twelve to fourteen days, by the house's own sheet, and the wine is then matured in French oak barrels, some new and some old, before it is blended and bottled at Sevenhill.
wine.glass: Blackberry and black olive over cassis, cedar and a touch of mint; medium in body and silky, with fine tannin and a dry, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage, it keeps for ten years and more in a good year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Sevenhill Cellars, the winery the Jesuits founded in 1851, names St Ignatius for the founder of their order. It is a Clare Valley blend of Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc: blackberry and black olive, medium in body and silky.
records.story: In 1848 two Austrian Jesuit priests reached South Australia as chaplains to a party of Silesian migrants. In 1851 the Jesuits bought land near the village of Clare and named it Sevenhill for the seven hills of Rome, and, as the house tells it, planted the first vines that same year, so that the Church in the colony need not buy its altar wine from Europe. A Jesuit brother is remembered for bringing the first vines from the Hawker family's Bungaree Station, and wine followed five years later, by the house's account; a Sevenhill wine took first prize at the Auburn show in 1858. Sacramental wine has been made at Sevenhill ever since, for parishes in Australia and overseas. Table wine grew beside it: the seventh Jesuit winemaker held the post from 1972 until he retired in 2003, and the house's reserve Shiraz carries his name. In 2026 the winery marked its one hundred and seventy fifth year, and it calls itself the oldest winery of the Clare Valley. St Ignatius, a blend of four Bordeaux grapes named for the order's founder, shows the house as a maker of table wine as well as of wine for the altar.

wine.name: Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the house's own vines.
wine.sites: The house's Cordon Cut vineyard at Auburn, near the cellar door in the old railway station, planted wholly to Riesling in a warmer, lower part of the valley than its Watervale vines; in 2017, when frost struck Auburn, the fruit came from Watervale.
wine.making: Once the grapes are ripe the canes are cut, so the bunches, cut off from the vine's water, shrivel and concentrate on the vine for some weeks before they are picked. No botrytis is involved: the sweetness comes from the drying alone. The wine is sold in half bottles.
wine.glass: Lime marmalade and candied lemon peel over apricot and honey; sweet and concentrated, yet lifted by bright, firm acidity, so it finishes clean rather than heavy.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its fresh lime, it keeps for ten years and more, turning towards marmalade and honey.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour, with a fruit tart or blue cheese.

label.means: The method: the canes are cut so the ripe grapes dry and concentrate on the vine.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The variety named on the label, here made sweet rather than dry.

records.table: Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut is a sweet Clare Valley Riesling made by cutting the canes once the grapes are ripe, so they dry and concentrate on the vine without botrytis. Lime marmalade and honey meet bright acidity; pour it cold, in a small glass.
records.story: The house takes its name from Mount Horrocks, which honours John Ainsworth Horrocks (1818 to 1846). Born at Penwortham Lodge in Lancashire, he founded the village of Penwortham in 1840, among the first European settlements of the Clare Valley, and he pioneered the use of camels in Australian exploration; in 1846, on an expedition to the north, his gun went off as his camel lurched, and he died of the wound. The wine house of his name was bought in 1993 by a winemaker who had sold fine wine in Perth, and in April 1998 the old railway station at Auburn was restored as its cellar door. The Cordon Cut vineyard lies close by, planted wholly to Riesling, and by 2014 the house counted more than twenty vintages of the wine; when frost struck Auburn in 2017, it was made from the house's Watervale fruit. The method gives the wine its name: once the grapes are ripe the canes are cut, and the fruit dries on the vine for weeks before picking. To a sommelier Cordon Cut is the valley's other face: a sweet Riesling from a region known for dry ones, sweet without noble rot.

cards.back: The canes are cut once the grapes are ripe, and the fruit dries on the vine for weeks.

cards.front: Which building at Auburn did Mount Horrocks restore as its cellar door in 1998?

questions.q: A guest asks how Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut gains its sweetness. Which answer is right?
opts: Canes cut so the grapes dry on the vine
Noble rot encouraged by autumn mists
Grapes frozen after picking, before pressing
questions.exp: The canes are cut once the fruit is ripe and the grapes shrivel on the vine; no botrytis is involved, so the noble rot answer is the nearest wrong one.

questions.q: Mount Horrocks takes its name from a pioneer of the Clare Valley. Which village did he found in 1840?
questions.exp: John Ainsworth Horrocks founded Penwortham in 1840 and named it for his family's Lancashire home; Sevenhill was the Jesuits' foundation of 1851.

The owner since 1993 is living and is not named; the story speaks of the purchase as history.

The house's place among the fourteen screwcap producers of 2000 rests on secondary accounts read through search summaries, with the Clare Valley Wine and Grape Association's page giving the fourteen but not, in the summary read, their names; the checker may test it or cut the sentence.
Horrocks's dates, Penwortham of 1840 and the camel rest on the Australian Dictionary of Biography and Wikipedia.

The plan calls it a Watervale house; its cellar door and the Cordon Cut vineyard are at Auburn and its dry Riesling vines at Watervale, so the place is Auburn. The plan's why says the canes are cut so the fruit dries on the vine, which the record keeps. No swap proposed.
